title: Earnings Desk: real quarters
teaches: Read real quarters the way a desk does: put the company's own numbers against the consensus, call beat, miss or in line, work the surprise in percent, then read the guide and the rest of the report, because a beat does not promise a rally and a miss does not promise a drop.

facts.quote: several groups track a “consensus” estimate that’s the average for all the analysts covering the stock.
facts.claim: The consensus is the average estimate of the analysts who cover the stock.

facts.quote: A company beats (exceeds) the estimate or misses (falls short of) the estimate based on how actual earnings or revenues compare to the consensus. If the number equals the estimate, it’s said to be in line.
facts.claim: Actual above the consensus is a beat, below is a miss, equal is in line, for earnings and for revenue.

facts.quote: But simply beating or missing estimates isn’t always what moves a company’s stock price.
facts.claim: A beat or a miss on its own doesn't always decide which way the stock moves.

facts.quote: Sometimes a company might beat estimates but provide a dour outlook for the future, leading the share price to drop.
facts.claim: A company can beat and still fall when its outlook disappoints.

facts.quote: During these calls, management might give more color on the quarter, take questions from Wall Street analysts and provide guidance on the company’s future prospects.
facts.claim: Management often gives its guidance on the earnings call.

facts.quote: Many companies announce their quarterly and annual results simultaneously in a press release and an 8-K (which includes the press release as an exhibit).

walkthroughs.title: Two numbers, one verdict
steps: Every quarter has two sides. The company's own numbers usually come in a press release, filed with an 8-K.
The other side is the consensus: the average of the analysts' estimates.
Above the consensus is a beat. Below is a miss. Equal is in line.
Then work the surprise: actual minus consensus, divided by the consensus, times 100.

walkthroughs.title: Netflix, April 2022
steps: Netflix earns $3.53 a share. The consensus was $2.89. An EPS beat.
But paid members fall by 0.2 million, against its own forecast of 2.5 million added.
And it guides to losing 2 million more next quarter. The stock plunges 35% in one day.
The beat was about the quarter just gone. Members and the guide were about what comes next.

walkthroughs.title: Meta, February 2023
steps: Meta reports EPS of $1.76. Analysts expected $2.22. On its face, a miss.
But $4.20 billion of restructuring charges sit in that number. Without them, EPS is $1.24 higher.
Revenue beats, the 2023 cost outlook comes down, and the buyback grows by $40 billion.
The stock closes up 23% the next day. Read the whole release, not one line.

questions.q: Netflix, first quarter 2022: EPS of $3.53. The Refinitiv consensus was $2.89. How does EPS read?
questions.why: A beat. Actual above the estimate is a beat, below is a miss, and equal is in line. $3.53 is above the $2.89 Refinitiv consensus. Last year's $3.75 does not enter it: beat and miss compare with the estimate. The $3.53 included a $162 million non-cash currency gain, so take care with the size of the beat.
questions.lesson_line: Actual against the consensus. Above is a beat, below is a miss, equal is in line.

wrong.Miss: below the consensus: $3.53 is above $2.89, not below it. Below the consensus would be a miss.
wrong.In line: near consensus: In line means equal to the estimate, not near it. $3.53 and $2.89 are far apart.
wrong.A miss: below last year: Netflix did earn $3.75 a year earlier. But beat and miss compare with the estimate, not with last year.

questions.simple: It is a beat, because $3.53 is above the $2.89 that analysts expected.

questions.q: Walmart, first quarter of fiscal 2023: adjusted EPS of $1.30 against $1.48 expected. That's a beat.
questions.why: False. It's a miss. Actual below the estimate is a miss, and the adjusted $1.30 is below the $1.48 expected. CNBC said Walmart missed by a wide margin. AP, using a Zacks survey, also put it far short of $1.48.
questions.lesson_line: Below the consensus is a miss. Get the direction right before anything else.
questions.simple: False, because $1.30 is below the $1.48 analysts expected, so it is a miss.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Actual EPS minus the consensus, divided by the consensus, times 100, is the earnings ___ in percent.
questions.why: Surprise. Zacks works it as actual minus consensus, over the consensus, times 100. Positive is a beat, negative a miss. When a loss is expected, Zacks divides by the consensus without its minus sign.
questions.lesson_line: The surprise in percent puts a beat at Netflix and a miss at Walmart on the same scale.

questions.q: Alphabet, first quarter 2024: EPS $1.89 vs $1.51 expected. Revenue $80.54 billion vs $78.59 billion expected. How does it read?
choices: In line on EPS and revenue
questions.why: Beat on EPS and revenue. EPS of $1.89 tops the $1.51 LSEG estimate. Revenue of $80.54 billion tops $78.59 billion. Each line is judged on its own, against its own estimate. Reuters also reported a beat on sales and on profit. Growth is a separate test: revenue was up 15% from a year earlier.
questions.lesson_line: Read EPS and revenue as two lines. Each one beats or misses on its own.

wrong.EPS beat, revenue missed: Revenue beat too: $80.54 billion against $78.59 billion expected.
wrong.In line on EPS and revenue: In line means equal to the estimate. Both numbers came in above it.

questions.simple: It beat on both, because $1.89 is above $1.51 and $80.54 billion is above $78.59 billion.

questions.q: Target, first quarter 2022: adjusted EPS $2.19 vs $3.07 expected. Revenue $25.17 billion vs $24.49 billion expected. How does it read?
questions.why: EPS missed, revenue beat. Adjusted EPS of $2.19 fell 88 cents short of the $3.07 Refinitiv consensus. Revenue of $25.17 billion topped the $24.49 billion expected. AP, using a FactSet poll, makes the same two calls. One line can beat while the other misses.
questions.lesson_line: A sales beat and a profit miss can sit in one report. Say both halves out loud.

wrong.EPS beat, revenue missed: That's backwards. $2.19 is below $3.07, and $25.17 billion is above $24.49 billion.
wrong.Missed on EPS and revenue: Revenue beat: $25.17 billion against $24.49 billion expected.

questions.simple: EPS missed and revenue beat, because $2.19 is under $3.07 while $25.17 billion is over $24.49 billion.

questions.q: An earnings story's "expected" number depends on whose analyst survey it quotes.
questions.why: True. Each outlet quotes a survey, and surveys differ. For one Netflix quarter, StreetAccount expected 2.73 million new members and FactSet 2.8 million. For Meta's next-quarter revenue, Refinitiv had $27.1 billion and Bloomberg's story $27.3 billion. FINRA notes that several groups track a consensus. On a close call, the survey you use can change the verdict.
questions.lesson_line: Know whose consensus you're reading. On a close call, the survey can change the verdict.
questions.simple: True, because each outlet quotes its own survey of analysts, and the surveys do not always match.

questions.q: Nike's fiscal Q4 2024 release says results "led us to update our Fiscal '25 outlook." No new numbers follow. Where do you find them?
questions.why: On the earnings call. Nike's release said only that results led it to update its Fiscal '25 outlook. It held its call the same afternoon, and finance chief Matthew Friend explained the guidance cut to analysts there. Schwab says that when the release has no guidance, look in associated materials or wait for the call. The consensus is the analysts' forecast, never the company's.
questions.lesson_line: Guidance isn't always in the release. When it's missing, check the call.

wrong.In the consensus estimate: That's the analysts' average forecast, not the company's own.
wrong.In the after-hours price: A price shows how the market reacts. It doesn't tell you what the company forecast.
wrong.In last quarter's release: It was written last quarter. It can't hold the outlook Nike just updated.

questions.simple: On the earnings call, because Nike's finance chief explained the new outlook to analysts there the same day.

questions.q: When a company gives its own forecast for a number, the quarter is also judged against that forecast.
questions.why: True. A company's own forecast is a second bar, beside the analysts' consensus. Netflix forecast 2.5 million new paid members for the quarter and lost 0.2 million. Its own letter set the result against that forecast. Schwab lists missing guidance as one way a company disappoints shareholders and analysts. It does not replace the consensus: check both.
questions.lesson_line: Two bars to clear: the analysts' consensus and the company's own forecast. Check both.
questions.simple: True, because a company that sets its own target is measured against it, and Netflix fell far short of its own.

questions.q: Alphabet, first quarter 2024: EPS $1.89. The LSEG consensus was $1.51. What was the surprise?
questions.why: 25.2%. The surprise is actual minus consensus, divided by the consensus, times 100. So $1.89 minus $1.51, divided by $1.51, times 100, is 25.2%. Positive means a beat. Zacks divides by the absolute value of the consensus, which only matters when a loss is expected.
questions.lesson_line: Work every surprise in percent. Then a big company and a small one read on one scale.
questions.simple: 25.2%, because you take $1.89 minus $1.51 and then divide that gap by $1.51.

wrong.20.1%: Divided the gap by the actual EPS instead of the consensus.
wrong.38.0%: Gave the gap in cents as if it were a percent.

questions.q: Netflix forecast 2.5 million new paid members for the first quarter of 2022. It lost 0.2 million. How far short was it?
questions.why: 2.7 million. Netflix forecast adding 2.5 million paid members and lost 0.2 million instead. The gap from plus 2.5 million to minus 0.2 million is 2.5 plus 0.2, or 2.7 million. It was Netflix's first decline in paid users in more than a decade. This gap is against Netflix's own forecast. StreetAccount's analysts expected even more, 2.73 million adds.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the miss against the company's own forecast too. Netflix missed its own badly.
questions.simple: 2.7 million, because it planned to add 2.5 million and lost 0.2 million instead, so you add the two.

wrong.2.3 million: Subtracted the loss from the forecast instead of adding.
wrong.2.5 million: Gave the forecast and ignored the loss.
wrong.0.2 million: Gave only the loss and ignored the forecast.

questions.q: Meta, fourth quarter 2022: revenue $32.17 billion, down 4% from a year earlier. Analysts expected $31.53 billion. How does revenue read?
questions.why: A beat, though sales fell. Beat and miss compare the actual with the estimate, not with last year. $32.17 billion is above the $31.53 billion Refinitiv estimate, so revenue beat. The 4% drop from a year earlier is growth, a separate test. Bloomberg also said sales fell and still beat estimates.
questions.lesson_line: Growth compares with last year. Beat or miss compares with the estimate. Keep the two apart.

wrong.A miss, because sales fell: Falling from a year ago is about growth. Against the $31.53 billion estimate, it beat.
wrong.In line with last year: In line means equal to the estimate. Sales were down 4% on last year and above the estimate.
wrong.Can't tell without EPS: Revenue is read on its own line. You only need actual and estimate.

questions.simple: It is a beat, because revenue came in above the $31.53 billion estimate, even though it fell from last year.

questions.q: Walmart, first quarter of fiscal 2023: adjusted EPS $1.30. The Refinitiv consensus was $1.48. By what percent did it miss?
questions.why: 12.2%. Divide the shortfall by the consensus and multiply by 100. $1.48 minus $1.30, divided by $1.48, times 100, is 12.2%. That shortfall is the 18 cents CNBC reported. In Zacks's formula a miss is a negative surprise, so it reads minus 12.2%.
questions.lesson_line: Put the miss in percent, so you can weigh it against any other quarter.
questions.simple: 12.2%, because the 18-cent shortfall divided by the $1.48 estimate comes to about 12.2%.

wrong.13.8%: Divided the shortfall by the actual EPS instead of the consensus.
wrong.18.0%: Gave the shortfall in cents as if it were a percent.

questions.q: Meta's Q4 2022 EPS was $1.76. Its release says that without restructuring charges, EPS would have been $1.24 higher. What EPS is that?
questions.why: $3.00. $1.76 plus $1.24 is $3.00. That is EPS without the $4.20 billion of restructuring charges, as Meta's release puts it. It is a what-if figure. Meta's reported EPS stays $1.76.
questions.lesson_line: When a big charge sits in EPS, work the number without it too. Then compare.
questions.simple: $3.00, because you add the $1.24 the charges took off back onto the reported $1.76.

wrong.$0.52: Subtracted the charges instead of adding them back.
wrong.$2.18: Multiplied the two numbers instead of adding.
wrong.$0.70: Divided the charges by the reported EPS.

questions.story: Nike, fiscal Q4 2024: adjusted EPS $1.01 vs 83 cents expected. Revenue $12.61 billion vs $12.84 billion expected. It guides fiscal 2025 sales down mid-single digits. Analysts expected a 0.9% rise.
questions.q: Which line in this report worries you most?
questions.why: The full-year sales guide. Analysts expected fiscal 2025 sales up 0.9%, and Nike guided them down mid single digits. Guidance looks ahead, and Schwab says it can often be the top factor in the near-term price. The EPS beat and the revenue miss are about the quarter just gone. CNBC tied the next day's plunge of nearly 20% to the guidance cut.
questions.lesson_line: Read the guide before you celebrate the beat. The beat is last quarter; the guide is the year ahead.

wrong.The adjusted EPS line: It beat: $1.01 against 83 cents expected. And it's the quarter just gone.
wrong.Nothing: EPS beat the estimate: A beat doesn't cancel a weak outlook. CNBC tied the plunge to the guidance cut.
wrong.The quarter's revenue miss: It matters, but it's one quarter. The guide marks down the whole year ahead.

questions.simple: The full-year guide worries most, because Nike now sees sales falling for the year while analysts expected a 0.9% rise.

reasons: the 0.9% and 83-cent consensus figures rest on CNBC alone

questions.q: Walmart, May 2022. New full-year guide: sales up about 4%, was 3%. EPS down about 1%, was up mid single digits. How does it read?
questions.why: Sales raised, profit cut. Walmart lifted its full-year sales outlook from about 3% growth to about 4%. It cut its EPS outlook from a mid-single-digit rise to a fall of about 1%. It expects to sell more and keep less. Its CEO blamed food and fuel inflation for the pressure on margins and costs.
questions.lesson_line: A guide can raise sales and cut profit at once. Read both lines before you call it.

wrong.A raise across the board: Only sales went up. The EPS outlook went from growth to a drop of about 1%.
wrong.A cut across the board: The sales outlook went up, from about 3% to about 4%.
wrong.Neither line really moved: Both lines moved, and the EPS line flipped from growth to decline.

questions.simple: Sales were raised and profit was cut, because Walmart now sees sales up about 4% but EPS down about 1%.

questions.q: Target, first quarter 2022: adjusted EPS $2.19. The Refinitiv consensus was $3.07. By what percent did it miss?
questions.why: 28.7%. Divide the shortfall by the consensus and multiply by 100. $3.07 minus $2.19, divided by $3.07, times 100, is 28.7%. That shortfall is the 88 cents CNBC reported. In Zacks's formula a miss is a negative surprise, so it reads minus 28.7%.
questions.lesson_line: Size every miss in percent before you judge it. This one was deep.
questions.simple: 28.7%, because the 88-cent shortfall divided by the $3.07 estimate comes to about 28.7%.

wrong.40.2%: Divided the shortfall by the actual EPS instead of the consensus.
wrong.88.0%: Gave the shortfall in cents as if it were a percent.
wrong.71.3%: Gave the actual EPS as a share of the consensus, not the miss.

questions.story: Walmart, first quarter of fiscal 2023. Revenue: $141.57 billion vs $138.94 billion expected. Adjusted EPS: $1.30 vs $1.48 expected.
questions.q: What does that mix tell you about the quarter?
questions.why: Sales held; costs hit profit. Revenue beat, so shoppers kept buying. Adjusted EPS missed, so the squeeze came between sales and profit. Walmart's CEO said food and fuel inflation put more pressure on margins and costs than expected. AP named labor, fuel and inventory costs. Adjusted EPS already leaves out the equity-investment swings. The costs the CEO and AP named are running costs. The stock closed down 11.38% that day.
questions.lesson_line: A sales beat with a profit miss points at costs and margins. Find out which, and whether they'll last.

wrong.Shoppers pulled back sharply: Revenue beat the estimate, so shoppers kept buying. The squeeze came below the sales line.
wrong.A one-time charge hit EPS: Adjusted EPS already leaves out the investment gains and losses. The miss came from running costs: labor, fuel and inventory.
wrong.A strong quarter all around: Profit missed by a wide margin. A sales beat doesn't make up for that.

questions.simple: Sales held up but costs cut into profit, because revenue beat while EPS missed, and Walmart blamed food and fuel inflation.

deeper.trap: The trap is to read a sales beat as a healthy quarter. Revenue tells you customers came. EPS tells you what was left after costs. When the two split, find the cost first. Walmart's CEO pointed at food and fuel inflation, and AP named labor, fuel and inventory. Then ask whether that cost will last into the next quarter.

questions.story: Netflix, first quarter 2022: EPS $3.53 vs $2.89 expected, revenue $7.87 billion vs $7.93 billion. Paid members fell by 200,000, against 2.73 million adds expected. It guides to losing 2 million more next quarter.
questions.q: What's the real news in this report?
choices: The EPS beat over the estimate
A currency gain inside the EPS
questions.why: Members fell, with more losses guided. Netflix lost 200,000 paid members where StreetAccount expected 2.73 million added. It guided to losing 2 million more. Subscriber growth had long been a key number for Netflix. The EPS beat looks back at the quarter just gone. Members and the guide speak to what comes next. The stock plunged 35% in one day.
questions.lesson_line: Find the key number for each stock. For Netflix in 2022, that was members, not EPS.

wrong.The EPS beat over the estimate: It's real, but it looks back. Members and the guide speak to what comes next.
wrong.The slight revenue miss: It missed, but only just: $7.87 billion against $7.93 billion. Variety tied the drop to the subscriber loss.
wrong.A currency gain inside the EPS: The $3.53 did include a $162 million non-cash currency gain, worth knowing. But subscriber growth was the key metric, and it went the wrong way.

questions.simple: Members fell with more losses guided, because member growth had long been a key number for Netflix.

deeper.trap: The trap is to lead with the headline line. EPS beat by a wide gap, yet the $3.53 held a $162 million non-cash currency gain, and it says nothing about growth. For Netflix, CNBC called subscriber growth a key metric each quarter. Find the key number for each stock before you read the beat.

questions.story: Meta, fourth quarter 2022: EPS $1.76 vs $2.22 expected. Its release says $4.20 billion of restructuring charges are in that number. Without them, EPS would be $1.24 higher.
questions.q: Before you call this EPS line a beat or a miss, what do you need to know?
choices: How the stock moved after hours
questions.why: What the $2.22 estimate included. Reported EPS of $1.76 includes $4.20 billion of restructuring charges. Without them it would be $1.24 higher. CNBC said the charges made the comparison with $2.22 difficult. Compare an estimate and an actual only on the same basis. If the estimate counted the charges, compare it with $1.76. If not, compare it with the figure without them.
questions.lesson_line: When a big charge sits in EPS, check what the estimate counted before you call a beat or a miss.

wrong.Meta's EPS a year earlier: That's growth, a separate test. Beat and miss compare the actual with the estimate, not with last year.
wrong.How the stock moved after hours: A price shows how the market reacted. It doesn't tell you what the estimate counted.
wrong.Whether revenue beat its estimate: Revenue is its own line. It can't tell you whether the EPS estimate counted the charges.

questions.simple: You need to know what the $2.22 estimate counted, because $4.20 billion of charges sit inside the $1.76.

deeper.trap: The trap is to pick a side fast. As reported, $1.76 is under $2.22. Add back the $1.24 and the picture changes. Neither call is safe until you know what the estimate included. Then read the rest of the report: revenue, costs and guidance.

reasons: the key rests on CNBC's judgment plus Fidelity's same-basis rule

questions.q: The bigger a company's EPS beat, the bigger the stock's jump the next day.
questions.why: False. Nike earned $1.01 against 83 cents expected, Netflix $3.53 against $2.89, and Alphabet $1.89 against $1.51. All three beat. Yet Nike plunged nearly 20%, Netflix fell 35% in one day and Alphabet rose 10%. FINRA says simply beating or missing isn't always what moves a price. The guide and the rest of the report can outweigh it.
questions.lesson_line: The size of the beat doesn't set the move. The guide and the rest of the report do.
questions.simple: False, because a beat can still bring a drop: Nike and Netflix both beat, then fell nearly 20% and 35%.

deeper.counter: Netflix is the sharpest case. EPS of $3.53 against $2.89 was a wide beat. Yet the stock plunged 35% in one day, after a revenue miss and a surprise loss of subscribers. A beat on one line can sit beside bad news on the line the market cares about most.

questions.q: A company that reports EPS below the consensus will see its stock fall.
questions.why: False. A miss usually hurts, but not always. Investopedia says a negative surprise will usually result in a decline. Meta's reported $1.76 sat below the $2.22 estimate, charges and all. Its revenue beat, it lowered its 2023 cost outlook, and it closed up 23% the next day. Weak earnings with upbeat guidance can lift a stock.
questions.lesson_line: A miss usually hurts, but the rest of the report can outweigh it. Read past the EPS line.
questions.simple: False, because a miss only usually brings a drop: Meta's reported EPS sat under the estimate, yet it closed up 23%.

deeper.trap: The trap is the word will. A miss usually sends a stock lower, so the statement feels true. But the price reacts to the whole report. Meta's charges clouded the EPS line, while revenue beat and the cost outlook came down. Read the headline, then read everything under it.

questions.story: May 2022. On Tuesday, Walmart's sales beat but its profit missed. You own Target, which reports on Wednesday.
questions.q: What does Walmart's report tell you about your Target shares?
choices: Sales beat, so retail is fine
questions.why: A warning about Target's costs. Walmart's sales beat, so its miss came from costs. A day later Target missed by 88 cents and blamed freight and transportation costs. CNBC said Target's miss confirmed the same story from Walmart. Target fell nearly 25%, and both had their worst days since 1987. A peer's report is a warning, not a certainty. Our own rule: hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R.
questions.lesson_line: When a bigger name in your group reports a cost squeeze, treat it as a warning for yours.

wrong.Nothing: they're separate companies: Separate companies, same kind of costs. Target's miss mirrored Walmart's a day later.
wrong.Sales beat, so retail is fine: Walmart's sales beat, and its profit still missed. Sales alone miss the story.
wrong.Target should win Walmart's shoppers: Walmart's sales beat, so there's no sign it lost shoppers. Its miss came from costs.

questions.simple: It is a warning about Target's costs, because Walmart missed on costs, not on sales, and Target may face the same kind.

deeper.trap: The trap is to treat each report alone. A big peer's report is news about the costs your stock may share. Walmart's miss came from costs, not lost shoppers. Target's own release a day later named freight and transportation costs. Weigh the peer read as a warning, never as a sure call on the next report.

questions.story: Two EPS beats. Nike, fiscal Q4 2024: EPS $1.01 vs 83 cents, revenue $12.61 billion vs $12.84 billion, full-year sales guided down. Alphabet, first quarter 2024: EPS $1.89 vs $1.51, revenue $80.54 billion vs $78.59 billion, first dividend.
questions.q: Which report carried bad news beyond the EPS line?
choices: Nike's: a revenue miss and a cut guide
Both: the market sells every beat
Neither: an EPS beat outweighs the rest
questions.answer: Nike's: a revenue miss and a cut guide
questions.why: Nike's: a revenue miss and a cut guide. Nike's revenue was $12.61 billion against $12.84 billion expected. It guided fiscal 2025 sales down mid single digits. Alphabet's revenue beat, $80.54 billion against $78.59 billion, and grew 15%. Nike plunged nearly 20%. Alphabet rose 10%, its sharpest rally since July 2015.
questions.lesson_line: Two beats, two opposite days. Read past the EPS line before you decide anything.

wrong.Alphabet's: dividends mean slower growth: Revenue grew 15% and beat. The dividend came with a $70 billion buyback, not a slowdown.
wrong.Both: the market sells every beat: Alphabet's beat was bought: the stock rose 10%.
wrong.Neither: an EPS beat outweighs the rest: EPS is one line. Nike's revenue missed and its guide was cut, and the stock plunged nearly 20%.

questions.simple: Nike's report carried the bad news, because its revenue missed and it cut its sales outlook, while Alphabet's revenue beat.

deeper.trap: The trap is to stop at the EPS line, where both reports look alike. Both beat. The difference sits below it. One revenue line missed and one beat. One outlook was cut, while the other company added a dividend and a $70 billion buyback. Read every line the same way for both, then compare.

reasons: Nike's consensus figures rest on CNBC alone

questions.story: Meta guides first-quarter 2023 revenue to $26 billion to $28.5 billion. Refinitiv's consensus is $27.1 billion. Bloomberg News cites an average projection of $27.3 billion.
questions.q: How does Meta's guide compare with what analysts expect?
choices: A beat: the top end is $28.5B
A miss: the bottom end is $26B
Can't say: a range isn't one number
questions.why: Midpoint $27.25B: between the two. Read a range at its midpoint, halfway between $26 billion and $28.5 billion. FactSet scores guided EPS ranges by their midpoint against the consensus. $27.25 billion is above Refinitiv's $27.1 billion and just under the $27.3 billion average Bloomberg cited. Both gaps are small, and Bloomberg called the range in line.
questions.lesson_line: Judge a guided range by its midpoint, and know whose consensus you're using. Close calls flip with the survey.

wrong.A beat: the top end is $28.5B: The top end is the best case. FactSet reads a guided EPS range at its midpoint. Read this one the same way: $27.25 billion.
wrong.A miss: the bottom end is $26B: The bottom end is the worst case. FactSet reads a guided EPS range at its midpoint. Read this one the same way: $27.25 billion.
wrong.Can't say: a range isn't one number: It has one to read: the midpoint, as FactSet uses for EPS ranges. Here that is $27.25 billion.

questions.simple: The midpoint is $27.25 billion, just above the $27.1 billion one survey expected and just under the other's $27.3 billion.

deeper.trap: The trap is to grab the end of the range that fits your view. The top end is the best case and the bottom end the worst. FactSet reads a guided EPS range at its midpoint, so read this one the same way. Then check whose consensus you hold. When the midpoint sits between two surveys, call it close, not a beat or a miss.

reasons: the $27.3 billion average rests on one report whose compiler is not named

conflicts: Survey providers differ. Netflix Q1 2022 subscriber adds: StreetAccount 2.73 million (CNBC) vs FactSet 2.8 million (Variety). Meta Q1 2023 revenue: Refinitiv $27.1 billion (CNBC) vs an average projection of $27.3 billion (Bloomberg via Fortune, compiler not named). q06 and q24 key exactly this. Every beat/miss key uses one named survey as CNBC printed it (Refinitiv in 2022-23, LSEG in 2024), never a mix. Facebook Q2 2018 was considered and left out: secondary reports seen in research put a $1.74 actual against $1.72 (Refinitiv) and $1.75 (Zacks), opposite sides of the line, and I could not verify either on a citable page.

Netflix EPS basis: CNBC writes 'Excluding items, the company earned $3.53', but Netflix reports one diluted EPS ($3.53, GAAP), and its letter says that figure included a $162 million non-cash F/X gain. Whether the $2.89 Refinitiv consensus modelled the gain is unknown. q01 keys only the direction (a beat, by a wide gap); q18 names the gain as a wrong choice, not as the story.

Netflix reaction timing: CNBC Apr 19 'cratered more than 25%' (after hours), Variety 'more than 22%' (after hours), CNBC Jul 19 'plunged 35% in one day' (the next session). Reveals use only the 35% one-day figure, credited to CNBC. CNBC's July story says the drop followed 'a miss on revenue and a surprise loss of subscribers'; q18 keys members as the real news because CNBC's April story and Variety both lead with the subscriber loss and the forecast of more losses, and the revenue wrong-note says it missed.

Meta EPS comparability: the release says EPS would have been $1.24 higher without restructuring charges ($3.00); CNBC says the charges make the $2.22 comparison 'difficult'. Other outlets cite a FactSet estimate of $2.26 (seen in research, not cited). q13 asks only the arithmetic; q19 keys 'unclear', never 'a beat'. q21 calls $1.76 vs $2.22 'reported EPS below the consensus', which is literally true, and the why says why it rallied anyway.

Meta reaction: CNBC 'almost 20%' and Bloomberg 'more than 20%' are after hours on Feb 1, 2023; Morningstar's 'closed up 23% at $188' is the Feb 2 close. Morningstar's page metadata shows 02 February 2023 with a 09:18 UTC stamp, earlier than that day's US close; the text ('Thursday's opening level', 'closed up 23%') only fits a write-up after the Feb 2 close, likely Australian date. Used only in reveals.

Walmart: GAAP EPS $0.74 vs adjusted $1.30; the $1.48 consensus is adjusted (CNBC), so q02, q12 and q17 compare adjusted with adjusted. The guide numbers in q15 are CNBC's wording; the release's guidance table (Feb. 17 vs May 17 columns) shows the same: EPS 'Increase mid single-digits' to 'Decrease about 1%', net sales 'Increase about 3%' to 'about 4%' in constant currency. CNBC also says Walmart fell another 7% the next day; not used.

Target: GAAP EPS $2.16 vs adjusted $2.19; the $3.07 consensus is adjusted. The release rounds revenue to $25.2 billion; CNBC's $25.17 billion is used in questions. 'Fell nearly 25%' is CNBC's report-day figure.

Nike: the release gives GAAP diluted EPS $0.99 and $1.01 excluding restructuring charges; CNBC's $1.01 adjusted matches the latter, so q14/q20/q23 compare $1.01 with the 83-cent LSEG consensus. Other outlets cited $0.84 (seen in research, not cited). The fiscal 2025 guide is not in the release (it says only that results 'led us to update our Fiscal '25 outlook'); CNBC attributes the guide to finance chief Matthew Friend on the call, which q07 keys. CNBC's 'plunged nearly 20% in trading Friday' was updated at 11:11 AM ET Friday; reveals say 'plunged nearly 20% the next day' as CNBC worded it, not a closing figure.
Alphabet: CNBC's Apr 25 headline says shares 'jump 14%' (after hours); the Apr 26 story says they 'shot up 10%' that session and closed at $171.95. Reveals use the 10% session move.
Surprise denominator: Zacks divides by the absolute value of the consensus; every consensus here is positive, so it equals the plain form used in q03, q09, q12 and q16.

Second publishers (checker, 2026-11-09): AP via WKMG ClickOrlando for Walmart (adjusted EPS $1.30 vs $1.48, Zacks survey; sales vs a $138.8 billion projection, a different survey from CNBC's $138.94 billion, a beat either way); AP via News 9 for Target ($2.19 vs $3.07, FactSet poll; AP's $24.83 billion is sales before other revenue, the release's total revenue is $25.17 billion, both beat); Reuters via RTÉ for Alphabet (same LSEG $78.59 billion; 'beat expectations for the quarter in sales, profit'). Nike's 83-cent and $12.84 billion consensus still rests on CNBC alone: other estimates seen in research (84 and 85 cents, $12.86 billion) sit on the same side, so the beat/miss direction holds, and q14/q23 key the guide and the mix, not the consensus figure.
Fortune's Target story (May 18, 2022) says revenue 'was a bit short' while printing $25.17 billion against $24.49 billion expected: an error on its face. Not cited.

Alphabet's $1.89 includes a $0.15 lift from equity-securities gains (release footnote). q04, q09 and q20 use the reported $1.89 as CNBC and LSEG compared it; without the lift EPS is still above every estimate seen ($1.49 Zacks, $1.51 LSEG, $1.53 Bloomberg).

Walmart f54 moved from CNBC to the release (Tier 1): CNBC's sentence mixed this quarter's adjustment with a prior-year divestiture loss. This quarter's adjusted EPS removes one item, equity-investment gains and losses ($0.56).

Meta next-day move: CNBC (Feb 2, 2023, updated 4:00 PM EST) 'jumped over 23% on Thursday'; Morningstar AU 'closed up 23% at $188'. Two publishers agree. Morningstar's piece also says a '$56 billion' buyback and a '$95-100 billion' prior cost range (the release: $40 billion, $94-100 billion), so it is used only as corroboration.

The why now states 'compare with the estimate, not last year', the rule q11 tests on Meta; that is teaching a rule before it is used on a new case, not giving q11's answer.

F5.02 teaches the surprise and works its formula (w1, q09, q12), so F5.02#q04 is kept; F5.08 keeps its real-quarter surprise drills (q09, q12, q16). The question stays in the file as the record.
